title: Reflection & Self-Critique
summary: Reflection wraps a generate step in a critique-and-revise loop: the agent produces a draft, an evaluator (often the same model in a critic role) judges it against explicit criteria, and the generator revises using that feedback — repeating until the critique passes or a budget is hit. This evaluator-optimizer pattern measurably lifts quality on hard, verifiable tasks, but each pass costs extra tokens and latency, so it pays off only when the critic can actually distinguish good from bad.
nestedConcepts: when reflection helps vs wastes tokens

subtopics.title: The generate → critique → revise loop
subtopics.explanation: Reflection adds a feedback cycle around generation: produce a draft, critique it, then revise the draft using the critique, and loop. Each iteration should make the output measurably better against the criteria. This loop is the whole pattern — everything else is deciding who critiques, against what, and when to stop.
subtopics.example:
draft = generate(task)
for _ in range(MAX_ROUNDS):
    critique = criticize(task, draft)   # judge the draft
    if critique.passes:
        break
    draft = revise(task, draft, critique)  # improve using feedback
# the loop keeps refining until 'good enough' or budget

subtopics.title: The critic is a separate role, not a separate model
subtopics.explanation: The evaluator can be the same LLM prompted to switch roles — 'you are a strict reviewer, find flaws' — rather than a different model entirely. The role switch matters: a critic prompt with concrete criteria surfaces problems the generator glossed over. Separating generation from critique in the prompt is what lets one model check its own work more objectively.
subtopics.example:
def criticize(task, draft):
    prompt = (
        "You are a strict reviewer. Check the draft against these rules: "
        "1) answers the question 2) cites evidence 3) no contradictions. "
        f"Task: {task}\nDraft: {draft}\n"
        "Return {passes: bool, issues: [..]}."
    )
    return llm_json(prompt)   # same model, critic role

subtopics.title: Evaluator-optimizer: measurable criteria drive revision
subtopics.explanation: Reflection works best when the critique is structured against explicit, checkable criteria rather than a vague 'make it better'. The evaluator returns concrete issues; the optimizer (generator) addresses each one on the next pass. Grounding the critique in measurable criteria is what turns reflection from wishful looping into a reliable quality gain.

subtopics.title: Stopping: pass, budget, or no-improvement
subtopics.explanation: The loop must terminate: stop when the critique passes, when a max-rounds budget is hit, or when a round produces no meaningful improvement (diminishing returns). Without a stop condition, reflection burns tokens forever or oscillates between two flawed drafts. A disciplined stopping rule is what keeps reflection from becoming an expensive infinite loop.
subtopics.example:
prev = None
for _ in range(MAX_ROUNDS):
    critique = criticize(task, draft)
    if critique.passes:
        break
    if draft == prev:            # no change -> stop, avoid oscillation
        break
    prev = draft
    draft = revise(task, draft, critique)

subtopics.title: When reflection helps vs wastes tokens
subtopics.explanation: Reflection pays off when quality is hard to get right in one shot AND the critic can actually tell good from bad — code that must pass tests, math with a checkable answer, writing judged on clear rubrics. It wastes tokens when the first draft is already fine, or when the critic is no better than the generator and just rubber-stamps or nitpicks. Judging whether a reliable evaluator exists is the key decision before adding reflection.
subtopics.example:
# GOOD fit: verifiable signal the critic can use
# - code -> run tests, critic reads failures
# - math -> check the numeric result

# POOR fit: no reliable signal
# - subjective one-liner where critic == generator
#   (extra passes add cost, not quality)

foundations.overview: Reflection (self-critique) is an orchestration pattern that improves output quality by looping generation through evaluation. Instead of returning the first draft, the agent generates, then a critic — usually the same model prompted into a strict reviewer role with explicit criteria — judges the draft and returns concrete issues, and the generator revises to address them. This repeats until the critique passes, a round budget is exhausted, or a pass yields no improvement. Framed as evaluator-optimizer, the evaluator scores against measurable criteria and the optimizer rewrites to raise that score. The pattern reliably lifts quality on tasks where correctness is hard to achieve in one shot but where a usable quality signal exists (tests to run, a rubric to check, an answer to verify). The crucial judgment is economic: every extra pass costs tokens and latency, so reflection is worth it only when the critic can genuinely distinguish good from bad — otherwise it adds cost without accuracy, or even degrades output by 'fixing' things that were fine.
foundations.formalDefinition: Reflection is an iterative refinement loop in which a generator produces a candidate output c0, an evaluator E maps a candidate to a critique (pass/fail plus specific issues), and an optimizer produces c_{i+1} = revise(task, c_i, E(c_i)); iteration continues until E signals pass, a maximum round count is reached, or successive candidates stop improving.
foundations.whyItMatters: Many valuable outputs — working code, correct proofs, on-spec documents — are hard for a model to produce perfectly in a single pass, and a second look catches mistakes the first pass missed. Reflection is one of the highest-leverage quality patterns available, but it also directly multiplies cost, so understanding when it earns its keep is essential to using LLMs economically.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a writer and an editor who are the same person wearing two hats. With the writer hat on, they draft quickly. Putting on the editor hat, they read critically against a checklist and mark problems. Then the writer hat goes back on to fix exactly those problems. The magic is the hat switch plus a concrete checklist; without a real checklist the editor just says 'looks fine' and the loop is pointless.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Coding agents that write code, run tests, read the failures, and fix them; math/reasoning agents that verify a computed answer before finalizing; content agents that check drafts against a style and factual rubric; and translation or summarization agents that self-check for omissions before returning.
commonUseCases: Code generation with a test suite as the evaluator
Math/reasoning where the answer is checkable
Long-form writing judged against an explicit rubric
Extraction/summarization checked for omissions or contradictions

commonMisconceptions.myth: More reflection rounds always improve quality.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Gains diminish fast and can reverse: after a point the critic nitpicks or 'fixes' correct content, and every extra round costs tokens. Bound rounds and stop on no-improvement.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A model can reliably critique itself on anything.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Self-critique helps only when a usable quality signal exists (tests, a rubric, a verifiable answer). Without one, the critic is no more reliable than the generator and mostly rubber-stamps or invents issues.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Reflection needs a second, different model.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The critic is usually the same model in a reviewer role with explicit criteria. A different or larger model can help, but the pattern works with one model and a good critic prompt.

interactiveExamples.title: A generate-critique-revise loop with a checkable signal
interactiveExamples.explanation: Generate a function, run a test as the evaluator, and revise using the failure until the test passes. The test is the objective signal that makes reflection worthwhile here.

code.caption: The evaluator runs real code, so its critique is trustworthy; the revision targets the exact failure and the loop converges in one round.
code.expectedOutput:
def inv(x): return 0 if x == 0 else 1 / x
passes: True

interactiveExamples.title: Bounded reflection that stops on no improvement
interactiveExamples.explanation: A general evaluator-optimizer loop with two stop conditions: the critique passes, or a round makes no change (to avoid burning tokens oscillating). This guards against the common failure where reflection loops forever without a hard signal.

code.caption: Two stop conditions keep the loop bounded: a passing critique, or a round that produces no change. Reflection without such guards can loop until the token budget is gone.
code.expectedOutput:
summary: raw (expanded with detail)
passed: True

codeLab.title: Build a bounded reflection loop
codeLab.instructions: Implement reflect(task, generate, evaluate, max_rounds=4). generate(task, feedback) returns a draft string (feedback is None on the first call, otherwise a list of issue strings). evaluate(draft) returns a dict {"passes": bool, "issues": list[str]}. Your loop must: (1) produce an initial draft with feedback=None; (2) evaluate it and, if it passes, return the draft immediately; (3) otherwise revise by calling generate(task, feedback=issues) and repeat; (4) stop after at most max_rounds evaluations; (5) ALSO stop early if a revision produces a draft identical to the previous one (no progress); (6) return the best draft reached even if it never passes. Complete reflect so the harness passes.
hints: Generate the first draft with feedback=None before the loop, then evaluate at the top of each iteration.
Return as soon as evaluate reports passes=True; that's the primary stop condition.
Track the previous draft; if a revision comes back identical, return immediately to avoid burning the whole budget oscillating.

checkpoints.prompt: When is reflection most likely to improve quality rather than just cost tokens?
options: When a reliable quality signal exists — tests, a rubric, or a verifiable answer — that the critic can use
Only when a second, larger model is available
checkpoints.explanation: Reflection helps when the evaluator can genuinely distinguish good from bad output (runnable tests, a clear rubric, a checkable answer). Without such a signal, the critic is no better than the generator and the extra passes mostly add cost.

checkpoints.prompt: This reflection loop can run forever. What's missing?
options: There is no round budget or no-improvement check, so a critic that never passes loops indefinitely
You cannot use while True with an LLM
checkpoints.explanation: The only exit is a passing critique. If the critic never passes (or the draft oscillates), the loop never terminates. Reflection needs a max-rounds budget and ideally a no-improvement stop.

checkpoints.prompt: How many revise() calls happen if the first draft already passes?
checkpoints.explanation: The evaluator returns True on the first draft, so the loop breaks before any revise() call. Reflection adds zero cost when the first attempt is already good — which is exactly why you check before revising.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the guard that stops the loop when a round makes no progress.
checkpoints.explanation: Comparing the current draft to the previous one detects when revision changed nothing. Stopping on no-improvement prevents the loop from oscillating or burning the budget without gaining quality.

theory.question: Describe the reflection (self-critique) pattern and the evaluator-optimizer framing.
theory.directAnswer: Reflection loops generation through evaluation: the generator produces a draft, an evaluator (often the same model in a strict reviewer role with explicit criteria) returns a pass/fail plus concrete issues, and the generator revises to address them, repeating until the critique passes, a round budget is hit, or a pass yields no improvement. The evaluator-optimizer framing names the two halves — the evaluator scores against measurable criteria, the optimizer rewrites to raise that score.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An iterative refinement loop that separates producing output from judging it, using the judgment to drive revision.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because models often can't produce hard outputs (working code, correct answers, on-spec writing) perfectly in one pass, and a critical second look catches errors the first pass missed.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Generate a candidate, evaluate it against explicit criteria to get specific issues, revise targeting those issues, and loop with a hard round budget and a no-improvement stop so it terminates.

theory.whyImportant: It's one of the highest-leverage quality patterns, but it directly multiplies cost, so knowing its mechanics and limits is core to using LLMs both effectively and economically.
theory.realWorldExample: A coding agent writes a function, runs the test suite (the evaluator), reads the failing assertion, and revises until the tests pass — reflection driven by an objective signal.

followUps.question: Why does the critique need concrete criteria?
followUps.answer: Vague 'make it better' feedback gives the optimizer nothing specific to fix; structured issues (missing test, unhandled case) make each revision targeted and effective.

followUps.question: Can the generator and critic be the same model?
followUps.answer: Yes — a role-switch prompt ('you are a strict reviewer') usually suffices; a different or larger critic can help but isn't required.

theory.question: Reflection costs extra tokens on every round. How do you decide whether it's worth adding, and how do you bound its cost?
theory.directAnswer: Add reflection only when a reliable quality signal exists that the critic can use (tests, a rubric, a verifiable answer) and when first-pass quality is genuinely insufficient; skip it when drafts are already good or the critic is no more reliable than the generator. Bound cost with a small max-rounds budget, a no-improvement early stop, and by reflecting only on outputs that fail a cheap pre-check rather than on everything.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cost/quality decision about when the marginal value of another critique-revise pass exceeds its token and latency cost.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Because reflection multiplies calls, and without a real evaluator the extra passes add cost without accuracy — sometimes even degrading correct output.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Establish whether a trustworthy evaluator exists; gate reflection behind a cheap check so only weak drafts get refined; cap rounds; stop on no improvement; and measure quality-per-token to confirm the loop actually pays off.

theory.whyImportant: It separates engineers who apply reflection reflexively from those who treat it as a measured cost/quality tradeoff, which is what production budgets demand.
theory.realWorldExample: A team gated reflection behind a fast lint/test pre-check so only failing code triggered the critique loop; quality rose on the hard cases while total token spend barely moved because most drafts skipped reflection entirely.

followUps.question: What's the failure mode of too many rounds?
followUps.answer: Diminishing then negative returns — the critic starts nitpicking or 'fixing' correct content, so quality plateaus or drops while cost keeps rising.

followUps.question: How do you prove reflection is helping?
followUps.answer: Measure a quality metric (test pass rate, rubric score) with and without reflection against token cost; keep it only where quality-per-token improves.

scenario.question: A team added a 5-round reflection loop to every answer in their assistant. Costs tripled but quality barely moved on evals. What went wrong and how would you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: They applied reflection indiscriminately and with too many rounds. Most answers were already fine (so reflection added cost, not quality), and where answers were subjective the critic — the same model — had no reliable signal, so it rubber-stamped or invented nitpicks. Fix it by gating reflection behind a cheap pre-check so only likely-weak answers are refined, cutting rounds to 1-2 with a no-improvement stop, and reserving reflection for tasks with a real evaluator (tests, verifiable answers, clear rubrics).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A misapplied-pattern diagnosis: reflection used everywhere and over-deep, without a trustworthy critic or a cost gate.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reflection is easy to bolt on globally, but its value depends entirely on evaluator reliability and on only refining outputs that need it.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Segment tasks by whether a real quality signal exists; gate the loop behind a cheap check so strong drafts skip it; cap rounds and add no-improvement stopping; then re-measure quality-per-token to confirm the fix.

scenario.whyImportant: It captures the single most common reflection anti-pattern and tests whether you can turn a cost regression into a targeted, measurable improvement.
scenario.realWorldExample: After gating reflection behind a confidence/test pre-check and dropping to two rounds, cost fell close to baseline while eval scores on the hard, verifiable subset improved — reflection now spent tokens only where it paid off.

followUps.question: How do you pick which answers to reflect on?
followUps.answer: Use a cheap signal — failing tests, low self-confidence, a lightweight validator — so only outputs likely to be wrong enter the expensive loop.

followUps.question: Why not just use a bigger model instead?
followUps.answer: Sometimes that's cheaper and simpler; compare a stronger single pass against reflection on quality-per-token, since reflection isn't always the most economical route to quality.

coding.question: Implement a bounded reflection loop that generates, evaluates against criteria, revises on failure, and stops on pass, budget, or no improvement.
coding.thoughtProcess: I generate an initial draft, then loop up to max_rounds. Each iteration evaluates the current draft; a pass returns immediately. If it fails, I compare against the previous draft to detect no-improvement and stop early, otherwise I revise using the specific issues. Falling out of the loop returns the best draft reached so the caller always gets something usable.
lineByLine: The first draft is generated with feedback=None so the generator knows it's the initial attempt.
The for-loop bounds the whole process at max_rounds, guaranteeing termination.
evaluate returns a pass flag plus concrete issues; a pass returns the draft immediately.
Comparing draft to prev detects a revision that changed nothing and stops to avoid oscillation.
On failure we save the current draft as prev and revise using the specific issues from the critique.
If the budget is exhausted without a pass, we still return the latest (best-effort) draft.
The __main__ demo converges in one revision once the critic flags the missing summary.
coding.timeComplexity: O(r) generate/evaluate calls where r <= max_rounds; each call is dominated by model cost.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) beyond the current and previous drafts.

followUps.question: How would you gate this to control cost?
followUps.answer: Run a cheap pre-check first and only enter reflect() when the draft looks weak, so strong first drafts skip the expensive loop entirely.

followUps.question: How would you use a separate critic model?
followUps.answer: Pass a distinct evaluate() backed by a different (often stronger) model or a real tool like a test runner, keeping the loop structure unchanged.

keyTakeaways: Reflection wraps generation in a critique-and-revise loop: draft -> evaluate against explicit criteria -> revise the specific issues -> repeat.
The critic is usually the same model in a strict reviewer role; concrete, measurable criteria are what make the feedback actionable (evaluator-optimizer).
Always bound the loop: stop on a passing critique, a max-rounds budget, and a no-improvement check to avoid infinite or oscillating runs.
Reflection improves quality only when a reliable signal exists (tests, rubrics, verifiable answers); without one it adds cost, not accuracy.
Gate reflection behind a cheap pre-check and measure quality-per-token so you spend extra passes only where they actually pay off.
